definition: False or fake, even though it may seem real, valid, or well reasoned.
example: The flyer quoted spurious statistics that no survey had ever actually produced.
nuance: Specious stresses that a false claim looks convincing; spurious just means it is false or fake, whether or not it looks convincing.
prompt: A researcher notices that ice cream sales and sunburns rise and fall together.
options: She called the link spurious, since hot weather drives both numbers up on its own.
Three careful experiments confirmed that the spurious link was real and direct.
The spurious discovery felt so lively and thrilling that the whole lab began to cheer.
Feeling spurious of the numbers, she rechecked every entry in the spreadsheet.
reasons: A third factor explains the pattern, so the apparent connection between the two is not real.
A connection that has been confirmed as real cannot also be false.
The word judges whether something is true, not how exciting or energetic it feels.
This mixes it up with suspicious; the word describes false things, not a person's distrust.

practice.prompt: A museum examines an old letter said to have been written by a famous explorer.
options: Written in a bitter tone, the spurious letter revealed how furious the explorer had felt.
Experts declared the letter spurious after learning its paper was made decades too late.
Because the curators thought the letter spurious, they displayed it as a treasured original.
The letter's graceful, looping handwriting struck everyone as spurious and beautiful.
reasons: A fake letter can't reveal the explorer's real feelings, and the word doesn't mean angry.
Paper that is too new shows the letter is a fake and not what it claims to be.
Nobody proudly displays a document as genuine after deciding it is fake.
Lovely penmanship says nothing about whether a document is fake.
